For own renderings (own_rendering: true) the field 'original' holds the exact source-language fragments as they stand on the page at 'url', so a machine check can match them; the English is my close rendering. Tertullian.org Dialogues pages carry page markers such as '|75' inside the text; none of the quoted spans cross one. The Hunter Blair Rule is an OCR text file: quoted spans were chosen so that no line-end hyphen or margin date falls inside them.

figures.name: Benedict of Nursia
figures.dates: c. 480 - c. 547 (traditional dates; the only early source gives no years)
figures.places: Nursia (Norcia) in Umbria; schooling in Rome; Enfide (Affile); a cave at Subiaco; Vicovaro; Monte Cassino
figures.role: Monk and abbot; founded monasteries at Subiaco and Monte Cassino; wrote the Rule that shaped Western monastic life
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches; declared patron of Europe in 1964. Cautions: almost everything known about his life comes from Book 2 of the Dialogues of Gregory the Great (written c. 593, about fifty years after his death, from four of his disciples). It is a book of miracles. A minority of scholars (Francis Clark, 1987) doubt that Gregory wrote the Dialogues at all. The Rule is Benedict's own, but it borrows heavily from an older anonymous rule, the Rule of the Master. The Rule allows beating boys and stubborn monks, which modern readers find harsh.
figures.hook: He walked out of the schools of Rome as a young man, lived three years in a cave where a friend lowered bread to him on a rope with a little bell tied to it, and later wrote a Rule so down to earth that it lets monks drink wine because, it admits, they cannot be persuaded to give it up.

stories.story: As a young student in Rome he saw many of his fellow students fall into loose living, so he gave up his books, left his father's house and went looking for a place to serve God. Gregory sums him up: he left 'instructed with learned ignorance, and furnished with unlearned wisdom'.
stories.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, prologue (P.W. 1608, ed. Gardner 1911)

stories.story: His old nurse followed him when he left Rome. She borrowed a sieve from the neighbours and it broke in two, and she wept because it was not hers. Moved by her tears, the young Benedict prayed over the pieces and found it whole.
stories.source: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 1

stories.story: He lived three years unknown in a narrow cave at Subiaco. The only person who knew was a monk named Romanus, who saved some of his own bread and let it down over the rock on a long rope with a little bell tied to it, so Benedict would hear it coming.
stories.source: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 1

stories.story: Tormented by the memory of a woman he had once seen, he nearly left the wilderness. Instead he stripped and threw himself into a thicket of briers and nettles and rolled there until his skin was torn. He later told his disciples that he never felt that temptation again.
stories.source: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 2

stories.story: A community of monks at Vicovaro begged him to be their abbot. When he held them to a strict life they put poison in his wine. He made the sign of the cross over the glass and it shattered. He told them calmly to find an abbot who suited them, and went back to his solitude.
stories.source: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 3

stories.story: A jealous local priest, Florentius, sent him a poisoned loaf. Benedict gave it to the raven that came daily to eat from his hand and told it to carry the loaf where no one would find it. Gregory adds that Benedict was far more sorry for the priest than grieved for himself.
stories.source: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 8

stories.story: In a famine he gave away all the goods of the abbey to the poor. When a subdeacon asked for a little oil, the cellarer kept back the last glass of it for the monks. Benedict, angry, had the glass thrown out of the window onto the rocks so that nothing kept by disobedience would stay in the house. The glass did not break, and he gave it to the man who had asked.
stories.source: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 28

stories.story: Totila, king of the Goths, tested whether Benedict was a real prophet by sending his sword-bearer Riggo dressed in the royal robes. Benedict called out to the impostor before he came near: 'Put off, my good son, put off that apparel, for that which thou hast on, is none of thine.' When Totila came in person, Benedict rebuked him to his face for his cruelty and foretold his death.
stories.source: Dialogues, Book 2, chapters 14-15

stories.story: His sister Scholastica, a nun, met him once a year. One evening she begged him to stay and talk through the night. He refused, because the Rule said a monk must not stay out overnight. She bowed her head and prayed, and such a storm broke that he could not leave. 'God forgive you, what have you done?' he said. Gregory's verdict: she could do more than he could, 'which loved more'.
stories.source: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 33

stories.story: Standing at his window at night, he saw a light brighter than day, and the whole world 'gathered as it were together under one beam of the sun' was shown to him.
stories.source: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 35

temperament.trait: Stern, and ready to use a rod
temperament.evidence: A monk kept wandering out during prayer. Benedict found him standing idle and 'strake with a little wand'. His Rule also says that children who make mistakes in chanting 'shall be whipped'.

temperament.trait: Quick anger at disobedience, generous to the poor
temperament.evidence: 'Then in an anger he commanded others to take that glass with the oil, and to throw it out at the window, to the end that nothing might remain in the Abbey contrary to obedience.'

temperament.trait: A rule-keeper who could be out-loved
temperament.evidence: He refused his sister's plea to stay the night because the Rule forbade it, and was 'heavy' and complained when her prayer kept him there.

Gregory notes that a friend found him weeping bitterly, which was unusual, 'for the man of God used not in his prayers to weep, but rather to be sad'. He was weeping because he foresaw the destruction of Monte Cassino.
His Rule promises 'nothing severe and nothing burdensome', fixes two cooked dishes so that a man who cannot eat one can eat the other, and allows wine because monks will not give it up.

To the monks who had just tried to poison him he spoke 'with a mild countenance and quiet mind': 'Almighty God have mercy upon you, and forgive you: why have you used me in this manner?' Of the priest who later tried the same, Gregory writes that Benedict 'was far more sorry for him than grieved for himself'.

genuine_lines.quote: Idleness is the enemy of the soul.
genuine_lines.translation: Ernest F. Henderson, Select Historical Documents of the Middle Ages (London: George Bell, 1910), on the Internet Medieval Sourcebook

genuine_lines.quote: and let him study rather to be loved than feared.
genuine_lines.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (Fort Augustus: Abbey Press, 1906), OCR text on archive.org

genuine_lines.quote: prefer nothing whatever to Christ.
genuine_lines.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)

genuine_lines.quote: And never to despair of the mercy of God.
genuine_lines.location: chapter 4, the last of the 'tools of good works'
genuine_lines.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)

genuine_lines.quote: Put off, my good son, put off that apparel, for that which thou hast on, is none of thine.
genuine_lines.work: Gregory the Great, Dialogues (Benedict's words as reported by his disciples)
genuine_lines.translation: P.W. (1608), re-edited by Edmund G. Gardner (London: Philip Lee Warner, 1911)

genuine_lines.quote: Go your ways, and seek ye out some other father suitable to your own conditions, for I intend not now to stay any longer amongst you.
genuine_lines.work: Gregory the Great, Dialogues (to the monks who tried to poison him)
genuine_lines.translation: P.W. (1608), ed. Gardner (1911)

misattributed.truth: Not in the Rule. It is a later summary of Benedictine life, popular from the nineteenth century. The Rule does balance prayer, reading and manual work (chapter 48), but never uses the phrase.
Widely quoted online as Benedict's, but it is not in the Rule and no early source for it was found. Treat it as a modern saying in his spirit, not his words.

misattributed.line: The idea that Benedict founded an 'order' of monks
misattributed.truth: He founded individual monasteries under his Rule. A Benedictine 'order' with houses joined together came centuries later.

opinions.position: Talk should be rare. The teacher speaks; the learner keeps quiet and listens.
opinions.side_note: Strongly on the side of silence as a discipline.
opinions.quote: For it becometh the master to speak and to teach, but it beseemeth the disciple to be silent and to listen.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Split. Introverts and contemplatives like it; most people today value open discussion and would bristle at 'the learner keeps quiet'. Gregory the Great warns that too much silence festers, which makes a good contrast.

opinions.position: Jokes, idle chatter and anything said to make people laugh are banned everywhere, always.
opinions.side_note: Against humour as a pastime. Compare John Climacus, who is just as wary of laughter.
opinions.quote: But as for buffoonery or idle words, such as move to laughter, we utterly condemn them in every place, nor do we allow the disciple to open his mouth in such discourse.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Very one-sided today: almost everyone, Christian or not, thinks laughter and joking are healthy. That makes it a vivid 'sparring partner' statement: few will agree, and those who do will feel seen.

opinions.position: In a community nothing should be private property: not even a book or a pen. Everything is held in common and given out by need.
opinions.side_note: The radical side: no personal ownership at all (for monks).
opinions.quote: More than anything else is this special vice to be cut off root and branch from the monastery, that one should presume to give or receive anything without the order of the abbot, or should have anything of his own.
opinions.translation: Ernest F. Henderson (1910)
opinions.today: Few would apply it to themselves, though many admire shared living. Works in a quiz only if phrased as an ideal ('the best life would own nothing privately'), which splits people.

opinions.position: Guests are to be received as Christ, and the poor and strangers most of all, because the rich get honour anyway out of fear.
opinions.side_note: The superior may even break his fast for a guest, so hospitality outranks fasting.
opinions.quote: in them Christ is more truly welcomed. For the very fear men have of the rich procures them honour.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Most agree in principle; the sharp part (favour the poor stranger over the important visitor) splits people more than it seems. Also bears on today's arguments about strangers and migrants, which could make it heated.

opinions.position: Correct faults gently and with judgment. Scrub too hard at the rust and you break the pot.
opinions.side_note: The moderate side of correction, though the same Rule allows beatings for the stubborn.
opinions.quote: let him act with prudence, and not go too far, lest while he seeketh too eagerly to scrape off the rust, the vessel be broken.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Nearly everyone agrees in the abstract. More useful paired against a tougher view, such as 'love means telling people hard truths bluntly'.

opinions.position: A monk who leaves through his own fault may come back, starting at the bottom, up to three times. After that the door is shut.
opinions.side_note: A middle position: generous, but with a hard limit.
opinions.quote: Should he again depart, let him be taken back until the third time : knowing that after this all return will be denied to him.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Genuinely split: 'three strikes' feels fair to many; others say forgiveness should have no limit (seventy times seven). A good, concrete statement.

opinions.position: Living alone with God is only for those who have first been trained for years in community. Beginners belong with others.
opinions.side_note: Community first; solitude is earned.
opinions.quote: not by the new fervour of a conversion but by the long probation of life in a monastery, have learned to fight against the devil, having already been taught by the solace of many.
opinions.translation: Ernest F. Henderson (1910)
opinions.today: Splits well in modern form: 'I grow more on my own than in a group' versus 'you cannot grow without people around you'. Climacus says something similar about who should seek stillness.

opinions.position: Idleness harms the soul. Manual work is part of a holy life, and monks are truly monks when they live by their own hands.
opinions.quote: then are they truly monks, when they live by the labour of their hands, as did our fathers and the Apostles.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Broad agreement that work is good, but a real split on whether rest, leisure and 'doing nothing' are good for you. Phrase it as 'free time with nothing to do is bad for me'.

opinions.position: Wine is not ideal for monks, but since they will not give it up, drink a moderate daily measure, never to excess.
opinions.side_note: Moderation rather than prohibition; a realist.
opinions.quote: And although we read that wine ought by no means to be the drink of monks, yet since in our times monks cannot be persuaded of this, let us at least agree not to drink to satiety, but sparingly
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Splits Christians: many are comfortable with moderate drinking, many evangelicals abstain. The wry tone is a great reveal line.

opinions.position: A good rule of life should ask nothing harsh or crushing; hardness is only for fixing faults.
opinions.side_note: The moderate side, against heroic austerity.
opinions.quote: We are about to found therefore a school for the Lord's service; in the organization of which we trust that we shall ordain nothing severe and nothing burdensome.
opinions.translation: Ernest F. Henderson (1910)
opinions.today: Most people today side with moderation. It separates well from the desert extremists and from Climacus, who warns that pampering the body makes it wilder.

opinions.position: Everyone, including the youngest, should be asked for advice on big decisions, because God often shows the best way to the young. The leader still decides.
opinions.quote: We have said that all should be called to council, because it is often to the younger that the Lord revealeth what is best.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Splits by age and temperament: many trust experience over youth. A fresh, non-theological statement ('the youngest person in the room often sees most clearly').

opinions.position: Birth and social rank count for nothing in the community: a free-born man is not preferred to a former slave.
opinions.quote: A free-born man shall not be preferred to one coming from servitude, unless there be some other reasonable cause.
opinions.translation: Ernest F. Henderson (1910)
opinions.today: Almost everyone agrees today, so it tells the quiz little on its own. Better as a reveal line than a statement.

opinions.position: Care of the sick comes before everything else, because they are served as Christ himself. The sick should in turn not be demanding.
opinions.quote: that they be served in very deed as Christ Himself
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: One-sided (everyone agrees). Use only as a reveal line.

opinions.position: When the community sells what it makes, it should charge a little less than the market, so greed does not creep in.
opinions.side_note: Relates to 'wealth'.
opinions.quote: let not the vice of avarice creep in, but let them always be sold a little cheaper than by men in the world, that God may be glorified in all things.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: A real split, and fresh: 'a Christian business should charge less than it could' versus 'charging a fair market price is fine'. Business owners will argue.

opinions.position: God hears a pure heart and tears, not many words. Prayer should be short and pure, and prayer together always short.
opinions.side_note: Agrees with Climacus on simple prayer.
opinions.quote: And let us remember that not for our much speaking, but for our purity of heart and tears of compunction shall we be heard.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Splits churchgoers: some love long, free prayer; others prefer short set prayers. Non-religious people will mostly shrug.

opinions.position: Do not give way to anger or seek revenge; make peace with anyone you quarrel with before the sun goes down.
opinions.quote: To make peace with an adversary before the setting of the sun.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Many agree; many others say you need time to cool off before making up. That makes 'settle every quarrel the same day' a decent split.

opinions.position: Grumbling is one of the worst faults in a community. Obeying with a grumbling heart earns nothing from God.
opinions.quote: Above all, let not the evil of murmuring shew itself by the slightest word or sign on any account whatsoever.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: A lively split: 'venting about work is harmless' versus 'complaining poisons a group'. Fresh and everyday.

opinions.position: Make joining hard and slow, read the rules aloud three times, then let the person choose freely. Once they commit, it is for life.
opinions.side_note: Relates to 'pilgrimage': Benedict despised monks who wandered from house to house.
opinions.quote: Behold the law under which thou dost wish to serve; if thou canst observe it, enter; but if thou canst not, depart freely.
opinions.translation: Ernest F. Henderson (1910)
opinions.today: Splits well: lifelong vows and staying put versus keeping options open and moving on when a place no longer fits.

opinions.position: A leader exists to help those under him, not to be above them.
opinions.quote: it beseemeth him more to profit his brethren than to preside over them.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: Widely agreed today (servant leadership). Reveal line rather than statement.

opinions.position: He left the Roman schools because of the loose life there, yet his Rule makes daily reading compulsory and hands every monk a library book to read cover to cover each Lent. Holy reading yes; worldly schooling no.
opinions.side_note: A middle position: reading for the soul, not for career or polish.
opinions.quote: And in these days of Lent let each one receive a book from the library, and read it all through in order.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: The split is between 'read to grow your soul' and 'read widely, including secular books'. Most modern readers side with the second.

opinions.position: Speak the truth from the heart as well as the mouth, and do not swear oaths.
opinions.side_note: Gives no ruling on hard cases such as lying to save a life.
opinions.quote: To utter truth from heart and mouth.
opinions.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed. (1906)
opinions.today: One-sided as stated. Not useful as a statement; Gregory and Climacus are much sharper on lying.

sparring.over: They chose him as abbot, then hated his strictness and tried to poison his wine. He left them.
sparring.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 3

sparring.over: Jealous of Benedict's fame, he slandered him, sent him poisoned bread, and sent women to dance in front of his monks. Benedict moved away rather than fight.
Benedict saw through the king's trick and rebuked him to his face for his cruelty.
A loving clash: rule against love. She wanted a night of talk; he wanted to keep the Rule. Her prayer brought a storm and she won.
In his Rule he calls wandering monks 'given over to the service of their own pleasures and the joys of the palate' and worse than monks who make their own rules.

figures.name: Gregory the Great
also_known_as: Saint Gregory the Dialogist (in the East)
Servant of the servants of God
figures.places: Rome (born to a senatorial family; prefect of the city; turned his family house on the Caelian Hill into St Andrew's monastery); Constantinople (papal envoy, c. 579-586)
figures.role: City prefect, then monk, papal envoy and pope; author of the Pastoral Rule, the Moralia on Job, the Dialogues, homilies, and about 850 surviving letters; sent the mission that converted the English
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches, Doctor of the Church; honoured by Anglicans and Lutherans. Cautions: his Dialogues are full of miracle stories that many modern readers find credulous, and a few scholars doubt he wrote them. The famous 'Angles and angels' story comes from English tradition written down a century later (the Whitby Life, then Bede), not from Gregory himself. He freed some slaves but also ran church estates that used them. He rebuked a bishop for teaching classical grammar. His list of seven vices is not quite the later 'seven deadly sins'.
figures.hook: Chosen pope in a plague year, he was getting ready to slip away into hiding when he was seized and carried to St Peter's to be consecrated, and he spent the next thirteen years writing letters about how the job had wrecked his peace while he fed Rome, bargained with invading armies and sent monks to convert the English.

stories.story: Plague killed Pope Pelagius in 590 and the people chose Gregory. He wrote to the emperor begging him not to confirm the choice, but the city prefect intercepted the letter. He ordered processions of prayer through the plague-struck city (an eyewitness said eighty people fell dead in one hour while praying). Then, as he prepared to go into hiding, he was seized and brought by force to St Peter's and consecrated.
stories.source: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1 (his deacon was in Rome and saw it); tr. Ernest Brehaut (1916)

stories.story: Before he was pope he saw fair-haired boys for sale in the Roman market. Told they were Angles, he said they had angelic faces; told their province was Deira, he punned 'De ira', rescued from wrath; told their king was Aella, he said 'Hallelujah' must be sung there. He asked to go to Britain himself. As pope he later sent Augustine and forty monks.
stories.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 2, chapter 1 (Bede says it comes from 'the tradition of our ancestors')

stories.story: In his own monastery a monk-doctor named Justus, who had nursed Gregory through his illnesses, was found on his deathbed to have hidden three gold coins. Gregory ordered that no one comfort him, and that he be buried in a dung heap with the coins while the monks cried 'Thy money be with thee unto perdition'. Thirty days later Gregory took pity on him and had Mass offered for him for thirty days, and he says the dead monk then appeared, released.
stories.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 4, chapter 55 (his own account)

stories.story: In Constantinople he argued face to face with Patriarch Eutychius, who taught that risen bodies would be 'impalpable, and more subtle than the wind and air'. Gregory pressed him with Christ's words 'Handle Me and see'. He records the debate blow by blow in his commentary on Job.
stories.source: Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job, Book 14, sections 72-74 (Oxford translation, 1844)

stories.story: Bishop Serenus of Marseilles smashed the pictures in his churches because people were worshipping them. Gregory wrote twice: praise for forbidding worship, blame for breaking the images, because pictures are how people who cannot read learn the story. Serenus's people had walked out on him.
stories.source: Gregory the Great, Letters, Book 9, letter 105 and Book 11, letter 13

stories.story: He sent 15 cloaks, 30 blankets, 15 beds and money for mattresses to an old people's home at Mount Sinai, in a letter to 'John, Abbot of Mount Sina' asking for his prayers because he himself was 'suffering shipwreck' in church business.
stories.source: Gregory the Great, Letters, Book 11, letter 1 (AD 600)

temperament.evidence: 'Moreover you are well acquainted with my ways, that I bear long; but if once I have determined not to bear, I go gladly in the face of all dangers.'
temperament.source: Letters, Book 4, letter 47, to the deacon Sabinianus

temperament.trait: Homesick for quiet; melancholy in office
temperament.evidence: 'For I have lost the deep joys of my quiet, and seem to have risen outwardly while inwardly falling down.' The Dialogues also open with him sitting alone in silence and sorrow, grieving for his lost monastery life (Dialogues, Book 1, prologue).

temperament.trait: Dry, cutting irony, even to the emperor
temperament.evidence: When the emperor Maurice called him simple: 'For by the use therein of the term simplicity they politely call me silly.'
'For many a year's circuit has gone by since I have been afflicted with frequent pains in the bowels', with fevers that left him struggling to breathe.
temperament.source: Moralia on Job, letter to Leander prefaced to the work

temperament.evidence: He had a dying monk shunned and buried in a dung heap for hiding three coins, then 'began to take compassion upon him' and had Mass said for him for thirty days.

temperament.trait: Slow to convert, by his own admission
temperament.evidence: He tells Leander that 'for late and long I declined the grace of conversion', staying in public life after he felt called.
temperament.source: Moralia on Job, letter to Leander

genuine_lines.translation: James Barmby, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: wherein both the lamb may find a footing, and the elephant float at large.
genuine_lines.work: Moralia on Job, letter to Leander (of Scripture as a river both shallow and deep)

misattributed.line: Non Angli sed angeli (Not Angles but angels)
misattributed.truth: The crisp Latin line is a later compression. Bede's account has Gregory say they have 'an Angelic face', and Bede says the story came from 'the tradition of our ancestors', a century after Gregory. Gregory's own letters never tell it.

misattributed.line: Gregorian chant was composed by Pope Gregory
misattributed.truth: The chant is named after him from the ninth century on, but the repertory took its known form in the Frankish lands in the eighth and ninth centuries. No reliable evidence links him to composing it.

misattributed.line: Gregory invented the seven deadly sins (pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath, sloth)
misattributed.truth: His list (Moralia 31.87) makes pride the root and names seven 'principal vices': vainglory, envy, anger, melancholy, avarice, gluttony, lust. The familiar list with pride and sloth inside it is a later medieval reshaping. Relevant to the site's deadly-sins quiz.

misattributed.line: The dove at his ear (in paintings) dictating his writings
misattributed.truth: A legend from the ninth-century Life by John the Deacon, not from anyone who knew him.

opinions.position: Giving to the poor is not generosity but paying back what is already theirs. Keeping the common gifts of God for yourself is a kind of slow killing.
opinions.side_note: The radical side on wealth: sharing is justice, not charity.
opinions.quote: For, when we administer necessaries of any kind to the indigent, we do not bestow our own, but render them what is theirs; we rather pay a debt of justice than accomplish works of mercy.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split, including along political lines: 'what I give the poor already belongs to them' versus 'what I earn is mine and giving is kindness'. A strong statement.

opinions.position: Keeping too quiet about a hurt makes it worse. Telling it calmly lets the pain drain away; closed sores hurt more.
opinions.side_note: Opposite in spirit to Benedict's praise of silence. Climacus agrees that stored-up resentment is worse than open anger.
opinions.quote: For, were the tongue to tell calmly the annoyances that have been caused, the pain would flow away from the consciousness. For closed sores torment the more
opinions.location: Part 3, chapter 14, the silent and the talkative
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree ('talk it out'), but a real minority prefers to keep hurts to themselves. A surprising Father on the 'modern' side makes a good reveal.

opinions.position: Anger that comes from a hot temper destroys wisdom, justice and friendship: it leaves you not knowing what to do or in what order.
opinions.side_note: Against anger from temper; see the next entry for his defence of anger from zeal.
opinions.quote: By Anger wisdom is parted with, so that we are left wholly in ignorance what to do, and in what order to do it
opinions.translation: Library of the Fathers, Morals on the Book of Job (Oxford, 1844)
opinions.today: Broadly agreed as stated.

opinions.position: There is a good anger that comes from zeal. If you love your neighbour as yourself, you should be as angry at their wrongdoing as at your own.
opinions.side_note: Relates to 'anger': he holds both that temper-anger ruins you and that zeal-anger is a duty. Climacus is far more suspicious of anger.
opinions.quote: For if we are bidden to love our neighbours as ourselves, it follows that we should be as angry with their erring ways as with our own evil practices.
opinions.translation: Library of the Fathers, Morals on the Book of Job (Oxford, 1844)
opinions.today: Genuinely split: 'being angry at other people's wrongdoing is a sign of love' versus 'mind your own faults'. Strong statement.

opinions.position: People must be corrected differently according to their temperament: the same advice that heals one person harms another. Sometimes a lesser fault should be left alone so a deadlier one can be fought.
opinions.side_note: The flexible, case-by-case side of correction. This is the whole plan of Book 3, the basis of the planned Personality Quiz.
opinions.quote: That sometimes lighter vices are to be left alone, that more grievous ones may be removed.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits people: 'let small faults go so you can deal with big ones' versus 'a wrong is a wrong, name them all'. Useful and everyday.

opinions.position: No one should grab leadership. A good person should flee it in his heart, but obey if truly called. Leading souls is the hardest art there is.
opinions.side_note: He lived it: he tried to hide from the papacy.
opinions.quote: he ought, when enjoined to undertake supreme rule, in his heart to flee from it, but against his will to obey.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many admire reluctant leaders; others say if you can lead, step up gladly. 'The best leaders are the ones who did not want the job' is a good statement.

opinions.position: Forcing people into baptism is wrong and useless. Win them by the sweetness of preaching; the forced convert goes back and is worse off.
opinions.side_note: Against forced conversion (here, of Jews in Marseilles).
opinions.quote: For, when any one is brought to the font of baptism, not by the sweetness of preaching, but by compulsion, he returns to his former superstition, and dies the worse from having been born again.
opinions.work: Letter to Virgilius of Arles and Theodorus of Marseilles
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost everyone agrees today that faith cannot be forced, so it is weak as a statement but strong as a reveal. Pairs with Hilary, who says the same.

opinions.position: Pictures in church are good because they teach people who cannot read. Keep them, but never worship them.
opinions.side_note: A middle way between image-breakers and image-worship.
opinions.quote: For to adore a picture is one thing, but to learn through the story of a picture what is to be adored is another.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 13 (1898), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits Christians: Catholics and Orthodox embrace images; many Protestants prefer bare walls. Phrase as 'art and images in church help me pray'.

opinions.position: Clergy should not teach pagan classics. He also refused to polish his own style, scorning the grammar rules of Donatus when explaining Scripture.
opinions.side_note: Against classical learning for church leaders; content over style.
opinions.quote: since the praises of Christ cannot find room in one mouth with the praises of Jupiter.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 13 (1898), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today, Christian or not, would disagree. A good 'sparring partner' statement: 'a Christian teacher should stay away from pagan myths'.

opinions.position: Do not tear everything down at once. Turn pagan temples into churches and let old feasts continue in a changed form, because people climb by steps, not leaps.
opinions.quote: For it is undoubtedly impossible to cut away everything at once from hard hearts, since one who strives to ascend to the highest place must needs rise by steps or paces, and not by leaps.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 13 (1898), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: A real split, far beyond religion: gradual change versus a clean break (think quitting a habit). 'People change best by small steps, not all at once' will divide people.

opinions.position: People were born free by nature, and Christ came to break our chains, so freeing slaves is a good and saving act.
opinions.side_note: He freed some slaves, but did not call for ending slavery and managed church estates that used slaves.
opinions.quote: it is a salutary deed if men whom nature originally produced free, and whom the law of nations has subjected to the yoke of slavery, be restored by the benefit of manumission to the liberty in which they were born.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Everyone agrees today; reveal line only.

opinions.position: He refused to have a hand in killing even enemy invaders, though he says he could have had the Lombard leaders wiped out. He negotiated instead.
opinions.side_note: The peace side, as a personal refusal rather than a general doctrine.
opinions.quote: if I their servant had been willing to have anything to do with the death of Lombards, the nation of the Lombards at this day would have had neither king nor dukes nor counts, and would have been divided in the utmost confusion. But, since I fear God, I shrink from having anything to do with the death of any one.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many think a leader facing invaders should use force; pacifists will cheer. 'Even against an invader, I would rather negotiate than kill' works.

opinions.position: Every lie is to be avoided. A lie told to help someone is a lighter sin, but the perfect will not lie even to save a life.
opinions.side_note: The strict side, softened only by calling the helpful lie 'lighter'. Climacus allows a lie to the perfectly truthful 'with fear'.
opinions.quote: This kind of lying also those that are perfect eschew with the greatest care, so that not even the life of any man should by deceit of theirs be defended
opinions.translation: Library of the Fathers, Morals on the Book of Job (Oxford, 1844)
opinions.today: Most people today say you may lie to save a life, so this is a strong, dividing statement.

opinions.position: Gluttony is not only eating too much. It is also eating too soon, wanting finer food, fussing over how it is cooked, and eating greedily.
opinions.side_note: Wary of pleasure in food; the enemy is fussiness as much as excess.
opinions.quote: It should also be known, that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways.
opinions.translation: Library of the Fathers, Morals on the Book of Job (Oxford, 1844)
opinions.today: The 'foodie' version splits people: 'caring a lot about fine food and cooking is harmless' versus 'being fussy about food is a small vice'.

opinions.position: Before the Judgment there is a purifying fire for small sins, such as idle talk, too much laughter, or neglecting the household.
opinions.side_note: An early statement of purgatory; Protestants reject it.
opinions.quote: But yet we must believe that before the day of judgment there is a Purgatory fire for certain small sins
opinions.translation: P.W. (1608), ed. Gardner (1911)
opinions.today: Splits Catholics from Protestants and many others. Doctrinal, so use with care; the list of 'small sins' (too much laughter) is a vivid reveal.

opinions.position: A holy man's patience is greater than all his miracles.
opinions.side_note: Virtue over wonders, though Gregory also recorded and believed many miracles.
opinions.quote: for I make no doubt, but that the patience of so worthy a man did far excel all his signs and miracles
opinions.translation: P.W. (1608), ed. Gardner (1911)
opinions.today: Most agree character matters more than wonders; the split is on whether miracles still happen at all.

opinions.position: Married Christians are both weak and steadfast: they cannot let go of all earthly things, yet they can still long for eternal ones. Please your spouse without displeasing God.
opinions.side_note: A sympathetic, realistic view of married life, rather than a low one.
opinions.quote: Wherefore the mind of married Christians is both weak and steadfast, in that it cannot fully despise all temporal things, and yet can join itself in desire to eternal things.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Mildly split; most modern Christians see marriage as a path to holiness in its own right, not a weaker one.

opinions.position: Some people are cheerful or gloomy by nature, not by circumstance, and each temperament has its own danger: the cheerful lean to lust, the gloomy to anger.
opinions.side_note: Directly useful for the planned Personality Quiz.
opinions.quote: But some are not made joyful or sad by circumstances, but are so by temperament. And to such it should be intimated that certain defects are connected with certain temperaments; that the joyful have lechery close at hand, and the sad wrath.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: People split on whether personality is fixed ('I am just a gloomy person') or shaped by circumstance.

opinions.position: Strict fasting is worthless if it makes you look down on others. Harmony with people matters more than bodily discipline.
opinions.side_note: Peace over austerity.
opinions.quote: Whosoever then afflicts his body, but forsakes concord, praises God indeed with timbrel, but praises Him not with chorus.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Widely agreed; reveal line.

opinions.position: Scripture has plain and deep senses at once, but do not force everything into allegory: Job's acts of mercy must be read as real acts.
opinions.side_note: Uses history, allegory and moral senses, but defends the literal where it matters.
opinions.quote: if these words be violently strained to an allegorical signification, we make void all his acts of mercy.
opinions.work: Moralia on Job, letter to Leander
opinions.translation: Library of the Fathers, Morals on the Book of Job (Oxford, 1844)
opinions.today: Splits readers of the Bible between 'mostly literal' and 'mostly symbolic'.

opinions.position: He loved the quiet contemplative life best and felt dragged from it into business, like Jacob given Leah when he loved Rachel.
opinions.side_note: Prefers contemplation, but accepts active service as duty.
opinions.quote: I have loved the beauty of the contemplative life as a Rachel, barren, but keen of sight and fair
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Splits introverts and doers: 'I would rather think and pray than run things.'

opinions.position: Grand titles in the church are pride. Anyone who calls himself 'universal priest' is a forerunner of Antichrist. He called himself 'servant of the servants of God'.
opinions.quote: Now I confidently say that whosoever calls himself, or desires to be called, Universal Priest, is in his elation the precursor of Antichrist, because he proudly puts himself above all others.
opinions.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 12 (1895), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: The general form ('big titles for church leaders are a sign of pride') splits people; the specific form touches Catholic-Orthodox arguments, so handle with care.

sparring.with: John IV 'the Faster', Patriarch of Constantinople
sparring.over: The title 'Ecumenical (universal) Patriarch'. Gregory called it proud and profane and wrote to John, to the emperor and to the empress about it.
sparring.source: Gregory, Letters, Book 5, letters 18 and 20; Book 7, letter 33

sparring.over: Whether the risen body can be touched. Eutychius said it would be finer than air; Gregory said it would be real flesh. Gregory reports the argument in full.
Policy toward the Lombards and the emperor's rebuke calling Gregory 'simple'. Gregory answered with sharp irony.
Smashing church images. Gregory rebuked him for breaking them.
Teaching classical grammar and pagan poetry. Gregory said he heard of it with 'groaning and sadness'.
Maximus got himself ordained bishop against Gregory's orders and had Gregory's letters publicly torn up.

portraits.title: Gregory the Great inspired by the dove, with his scribe, from the Registrum Gregorii
Saint Gregory the Great
portraits.artist: Jusepe de Ribera (formerly attributed to Carlo Saraceni)

figures.name: John Climacus
figures.dates: c. 579 - c. 659 (an older reckoning gives c. 525 - c. 606; his dates are disputed)
figures.places: Mount Sinai (arrived young, trained under the elder Martyrius); forty years as a hermit at Tholas, about five miles from the monastery; visited monasteries near Alexandria; later abbot of Sinai (the monastery now called St Catherine's)
figures.role: Hermit, then abbot of Sinai; author of The Ladder of Divine Ascent, thirty 'steps' of the spiritual life, written at the request of John, abbot of Raithu; also a short treatise To the Shepherd
figures.status_note: Saint in the Orthodox and Catholic churches. The Orthodox Church reads the Ladder in monasteries during Lent and keeps the fourth Sunday of Lent in his honour. Cautions: his dates are uncertain; his short Life (by Daniel, a monk of Raithu) is devotional. The Ladder was written for monks, so its hard sayings about parents, laughter and the body are addressed to people who had left the world; he himself tells married people they can be saved. No public-domain English translation could be found online (the English lines circulating online come from the 1959 and 1982 translations, which are copyrighted), so every line below is my own close rendering of the Greek text in Migne, Patrologia Graeca 88, with the Greek given alongside.
figures.hook: After forty years alone in the Sinai desert he was mocked by jealous monks as a chatterbox, so he stopped teaching altogether until the same monks begged him to speak again; they later made him abbot by force, and the ladder of thirty rungs he wrote is still read in Orthodox monasteries every Lent.

stories.story: Envious monks called him 'talkative and a babbler' because so many came to him for teaching. Rather than argue, he fell silent and stopped teaching. His critics, ashamed of what they had cost everyone, joined the others in begging him to speak again, and he at once gave in. The monks later put him on the abbot's throne by force.
stories.source: Daniel of Raithu, Life of John Climacus (Greek in Migne, PG 88.596-608); modern Greek translation on the page given

stories.story: His disciple Moses, worn out from carrying soil for a vegetable garden in the August heat, fell asleep in the shade of a huge rock. At that moment John, dozing in his cell, dreamed that a venerable man shook him awake and asked how he could sleep while Moses was in danger; he woke and prayed. Moses said he seemed to hear John's voice calling him, jumped away, and saw the rock break loose and fall where he had lain. John said nothing about his vision.
stories.source: Daniel of Raithu, Life of John Climacus

stories.story: As a hermit he ate everything monks were allowed, but very little of it: little food to fight pride, and a bit of everything so as not to stand out and grow vain.
stories.source: Daniel of Raithu, Life of John Climacus

stories.story: At a large monastery near Alexandria he met Isidore, a former magistrate of the city, harsh and arrogant by nature. The abbot put him at the gate for seven years with orders to bow to everyone who came in or went out and say, 'Pray for me, father, for I am an epileptic.' Isidore became so humble that when the abbot wanted to ordain him he begged to be left at the gate.
stories.source: Ladder, Step 4, On obedience (PG 88.689)

stories.story: Near the same monastery was a house called 'the Prison', where monks who had fallen into grave sin lived in darkness and stench, doing penance. John stayed there thirty days and came back so changed that the abbot saw it at once in his face.
stories.source: Ladder, Step 5, On repentance

stories.story: When he was young, the great elder Anastasius saw him with his teacher Martyrius and asked who had given this youth the monk's habit. Told it was Martyrius, he exclaimed that Martyrius had tonsured the future abbot of Sinai. Forty years later it came true.
stories.source: Other biographical notes printed with the Life (from the Sinai tradition)

temperament.evidence: Accused of talking too much, he did not defend himself but went silent until his critics begged him to teach again, and then gave way at once.
temperament.source: Daniel of Raithu, Life of John Climacus

temperament.trait: A sharp, witty observer of people
temperament.evidence: His Ladder is full of 'I have seen...' sketches and one-liners. Of gluttony: 'Gluttony is hypocrisy of the stomach: when it is full it cries out that it is in need' (Step 14).
He calls himself and his like 'the unlearned' at the start of the Ladder, and says he returned from the Prison 'impatient' (ho anypomonetos).
He tells new monks not to pity the tears of their parents, and compares relatives who come to call them home to a swarm of wasps.

genuine_lines.quote: A Christian is an imitation of Christ, as far as that is possible for human beings, in words and deeds and thought, believing rightly and blamelessly in the Holy Trinity.
original: Χριστιανός ἐστιν, μίμημα Χριστοῦ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἀνθρώπων, λόγοις, καὶ ἔργοις, καὶ ἐννοίᾳ εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν Τριάδα ὀρθῶς καὶ ἀμέμπτως πιστεύων.
genuine_lines.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88

genuine_lines.quote: Blessed is the one who has come to such love for God as a lover mad with love has for his beloved.
original: Μακάριος ὅστις τοιοῦτον πρὸς Θεὸν ἐκτήσατο ἔρωτα, οἷον μανικὸς ἐραστὴς πρὸς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἐρωμένην κέκτηται.
genuine_lines.location: Step 30, On faith, hope and love
genuine_lines.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88

genuine_lines.quote: God is love; and whoever wants to define it is a blind man trying to measure the sand in the depths of the sea.
original: Ἀγάπη ὁ Θεός ἐστιν, ὁ ὅρον δὲ τούτου λέγειν βουλόμενος, ἐν ἀβύσσῳ τυφλώττων τὸν ψάμμον μετρεῖ.
genuine_lines.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88

genuine_lines.quote: Whoever flatters a lion often tames it; but whoever pampers the body makes it wilder.
original: Λέοντα ὁ κολακεύσας, πολλάκις ἡμέρωσε· σῶμα δὲ ὁ θεραπεύσας ἐπὶ πλείω ἠγρίωσε.
genuine_lines.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88

genuine_lines.quote: Gluttony is hypocrisy of the stomach: when it is full, it cries out that it is in need.
original: Γαστριμαργία ἐστὶν κοιλίας ὑπόκρισις· κεκορεσμένη γὰρ οὖσα ἔνδειαν ἀναβοᾷ,
genuine_lines.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88

misattributed.line: Gregory the Great's letter 'To John, Abbot of Mount Sina' (AD 600) as a letter to John Climacus
misattributed.truth: Some older writers identify this John with Climacus. On the later dating of Climacus (born c. 579) he would not yet have been abbot in 600, so the identification is uncertain at best.

misattributed.line: Popular online wording of Ladder sayings
misattributed.truth: Not misattributed, but the English usually quoted comes from the Lazarus Moore (1959) or Luibheid and Russell (1982) translations, which are copyrighted. The site should use fresh renderings of the Greek.

opinions.position: Married people living in the world can be saved by ordinary goodness: do all the good you can, speak ill of no one, steal nothing, lie to no one, keep coming to church, pity the needy, be faithful to your own spouse. But a married life is like walking with chains on hands and feet: possible, but hard.
opinions.side_note: A mixed position: salvation is open to the married, but the monastic road is easier.
opinions.quote: Do all the good you can; revile no one; steal from no one; lie to no one... do not stay away from the church's gatherings; have compassion on the needy; cause no one to stumble; do not go near another man's portion, and be content with your own wives. If you do this, you will not be far from the kingdom of heaven.
original: Πάντα ὅσα δύνασθε ποιεῖν ἀγαθὰ, ποιήσατε· μηδένα λοιδορήσητε· μηδένα κλέψητε· μηδενὶ ψεύσησθε·

μηδένα μισήσητε· τῶν συνάξεων μὴ χωρίζησθε· τοῖς δεομένοις συμπαθήσατε· μηδένα σκανδαλίσητε· ἀλλοτρίᾳ μερίδι μὴ προσεγγίσητε· καὶ ἀρκεῖσθε τοῖς ὀψωνίοις τῶν γυναικῶν ὑμῶν. Ἐὰν οὕτως ποιήσητε, οὐ μακρὰν
ἔσεσθε τῆς βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν.
opinions.location: Step 1 (PG 88.640-641); the omitted words are 'be proud toward no one; hate no one'
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: The 'ordinary goodness is enough to be saved' reading splits Christians (many insist on faith, not goodness) and appeals to many non-Christians. The 'chains' image splits married people.

opinions.position: If God calls you, do not let your parents' or friends' tears hold you back. Longing for God should put out longing for family.
opinions.side_note: The hard side: calling over family.
opinions.quote: Do not pity the tears of parents or friends; otherwise you will weep forever.
original: Μὴ οἰκτειρήσῃς γονέων ἢ φίλων δάκρυα· εἰ δὲ μὴ, αἰωνίως μέλλεις δακρύειν.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Strongly split, and a vivid 'sparring partner' line: most people today put family first; a minority believe a calling can override family wishes.

opinions.position: The goal is not just to hold anger in but to lose the taste for being honoured: to want insults the way the vain want praise. Meekness is a mind that stays the same under insult and praise.
opinions.side_note: The far end against anger; contrast Gregory's defence of zealous anger.
opinions.quote: Freedom from anger, then, is an insatiable appetite for dishonour, just as in the vainglorious there is a boundless appetite for praise.
original: Ἀοργησία τοίνυν ἐστὶν ἔφεσις ἀτιμίας ἀκόρεστος, ὡς ἐν τοῖς κενοδόξοις εὐφημίας ἀπέραντος.
opinions.location: Step 8, On freedom from anger and on meekness (PG 88.828)
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Almost no one today wants to be insulted, so this is a striking, divisive line. As a statement: 'A truly peaceful person does not mind being insulted at all.'

opinions.position: Swallowed resentment is worse than an outburst. He pitied people who kept quiet and stored up grudges more than people who raged; sometimes an explosion even clears out an old grudge.
opinions.side_note: Agrees with Gregory that bottled feelings fester.
opinions.quote: And I have seen people who seemed patient, but without reason, and through their silence stored up resentment inside; and I pitied them more than those who rage.
original: Καὶ εἶδον τὸ δοκεῖν μακροθυμήσαντας ἀλόγως, καὶ ἐκ τῆς σιωπῆς μνησικακίαν ἔνδον ἀποθεμένους, καὶ τῶν μαινομένων μᾶλλον αὐτοὺς ἐταλάνισα
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Many agree ('bottling it up is worse'); others think holding your tongue is always better. A good, everyday statement.

opinions.position: Music in the right measure can calm anger beautifully; out of measure or at the wrong time, it feeds the love of pleasure.
opinions.side_note: A moderate view of music: useful, but only in measure.
opinions.quote: Sometimes melody, when it is measured, dissolves anger excellently; at other times, when it is unmeasured and untimely, it keeps company with the love of pleasure.
original: Ποτὲ μὲν ἡ μελῳδία τὸν θυμὸν ἀρίστως διαλύει, ἡ σύμμετρος· ποτὲ δὲ τῇ φιληδονίᾳ συνέρχεται, ἥγε ἄμετρος καὶ ἄκαιρος.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Most agree music can calm; the split is on 'music just for pleasure is a spiritual danger'.

opinions.position: Correct with gentle teaching and patient rebuke, never with blows; if blows are ever needed, rarely, and never by your own hand.
opinions.side_note: The gentle side; contrast Benedict, who struck a monk with a rod and whose Rule allows beatings.
opinions.quote: 'Reprove, rebuke, exhort,' it says, but not 'strike'. And if even that should be needed, let it be rarely, and not by your own hand.
original: Ἔλεγξον, φησὶν, ἐπιτίμησον, παρακάλεσον· οὐ μέντοι καὶ τύψον. Εἰ δὲ καὶ τοῦτο δέοι, σπανίως καὶ οὐ δι᾿ ἑαυτοῦ.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Physical punishment splits parents today; most reject it, a sizeable minority accept it. A clean Benedict-versus-Climacus contrast.

opinions.position: Never condemn anyone, not even someone you see sinning at the moment of death, because God's judgment is hidden. He saw a man sin openly and repent in secret.
opinions.side_note: The absolute side of 'do not judge'.
opinions.quote: Even if you see someone falling at the very moment of his departure from this life, do not condemn him even then. For the judgment of God is hidden from men.
original: κἂν ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ἐξόδῳ τινὰ θεάσῃ πταίοντα, μὴ τότε αὐτὸν κατάκρινε. Ἄδηλον γὰρ ἀνθρώποις τὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ κρῖμα καθέστηκεν.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Split: 'we should never judge anyone' versus 'some things must be called wrong, and people with them'. A strong statement.

opinions.position: Silence brings you close to God; a talker does not yet know himself.
opinions.side_note: On the side of silence, like Benedict; contrast Hilary, who says silence can be cowardice.
opinions.quote: The friend of silence draws near to God, and, speaking with Him in secret, is enlightened by God.
original: Ὁ σιωπῆς φίλος προσεγγίζει Θεῷ, καὶ λεληθότως συνομιλῶν φωτίζεται παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Splits introverts and extroverts: 'I meet God more in quiet than in talk.'

opinions.position: Liars love to excuse themselves by 'the greater good' and compare themselves to Rahab. Only someone who has become completely free of lying may ever tell an untruth, and then with fear, when the moment truly calls for it.
opinions.side_note: A nuanced side: deeply suspicious of excuses, yet not an absolute ban. Stricter in practice than most people, looser in principle than Gregory.
opinions.quote: The maker of lies pleads 'the greater good', and often counts the ruin of his soul as righteousness... When we have become entirely clean of lying, then, with fear, and when the moment calls for it, we may resort to it.
original: προφασίζεται οἰκονομίας ὁ ψεύδους προβολεὺς, καὶ δικαιοσύνας πολλάκις λογίζεται τὰς ψυχῆς ἀπωλείας.
Ὁπόταν ψεύδους εἰς ἅπαν καθαρεύσωμεν, τότε αὐτὸ μετὰ φόβου καὶ καιροῦ καλοῦντος ὑπέλθωμεν.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88; 'the greater good' renders oikonomia (a lie told by 'arrangement' for someone's benefit)
opinions.today: Most people accept white lies and life-saving lies; his 'only the perfectly honest may lie' is unusual and memorable.

opinions.position: Laughter is the opposite of humility; holy sorrow and tears go with it. Rule your heart like a king: send laughter away and call sweet weeping in.
opinions.side_note: Against laughter, like Benedict, though he speaks of a 'spiritual laughter' of the soul for those who mourn well.
opinions.quote: If nothing goes along with humility as mourning does, then surely nothing opposes it as laughter does.
original: Εἰ οὐδὲν οὕτω τῇ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ ὡς τὸ πένθος συνέρχεται, οὐδὲν πάντως αὐτῇ ὡς ὁ γέλως ἀνθέστηκεν.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Very one-sided today (almost everyone values laughter), so it makes a vivid sparring line.

opinions.position: The best spiritual state is a sorrow for sin that is also full of joy, 'joy-grief'. Hold on to it.
opinions.side_note: Relates to 'grief' and 'emotions'.
opinions.quote: Hold fast, hold fast to the blessed joy-grief of holy compunction.
original: Κατέχων κάτεχε τὴν μακαρίαν τῆς ὁσίας κατανύξεως χαρμολύπην·
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88; 'joy-grief' renders charmolypē
opinions.today: Few people have a name for it; a statement like 'the best tears are happy and sad at once' divides the sentimental from the practical.

opinions.position: Pamper the body and it grows wilder. Gluttony pretends to be hungry when full and even uses a guest's visit as an excuse to feast.
opinions.side_note: The strict side; contrast Benedict's moderation.
opinions.quote: Whoever flatters a lion often tames it; but whoever pampers the body makes it wilder.
original: Λέοντα ὁ κολακεύσας, πολλάκις ἡμέρωσε· σῶμα δὲ ὁ θεραπεύσας ἐπὶ πλείω ἠγρίωσε.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Split: 'treat yourself' culture versus discipline culture. 'The more I indulge myself, the more I want' will divide people.

opinions.position: Solitude is not for everyone. Anyone troubled by anger, conceit, hypocrisy or grudges should not even think of it; for them it breeds more anger and resentment. Some lazy souls are saved by living among others.
opinions.side_note: Solitude only for the healed; community for most. Agrees with Benedict.
opinions.quote: Let no one who is troubled by anger and conceit, by hypocrisy and resentment, dare to look even at a footprint of stillness, lest he gain nothing but madness.
original: Μηδεὶς ὑπὸ θυμοῦ καὶ οἰήσεως, ὑποκρίσεώς τε καὶ μνησικακίας ὀχλούμενος, ἴχνος ἡσυχίας ἰδεῖν τολμῆσαι μήπως ἔκστασιν, καὶ μόνον κερδήσῃ.
opinions.location: Step 27, On stillness of body and soul
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Resonates today: 'time alone makes some people worse, not better.' Splits those who recharge alone from those who spiral alone.

opinions.position: You cannot beat your own body's desires by your own strength; only God can. Admit your weakness and chastity comes as a gift.
opinions.side_note: The grace side.
opinions.quote: Whoever wants to fight his own flesh, or to conquer it by himself, runs in vain.
original: Ὁ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ σάρκα βουληθεὶς πολεμῆσαι, ἢ νικῆσαι ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ, εἰς μάτην τρέχει.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Splits: 'willpower is enough' versus 'I cannot change without help from outside myself'. Also resonates with recovery culture.

opinions.position: Do not try to be clever in prayer. Children's simple stammering often wins over their Father; one word from the tax collector was enough. Many words scatter the mind.
opinions.side_note: Agrees with Benedict on short prayer.
opinions.quote: Do not be clever in the words of your prayer; for the simple, unadorned stammerings of children have often won over their Father in heaven.
original: Μὴ σοφίζου ἐν εὐχῆς σου ῥήμασι· παίδων γὰρ πολλάκις ἁπλᾶ ψελλίσματα καὶ ἀποίκιλα τὸν Πατέρα αὐτῶν, τὸν ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς ἐθεράπευσαν.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Most believers agree; the split is with those who love rich written liturgy or eloquent free prayer.

opinions.position: Keep your own death in mind every day. It is as necessary to the soul as bread to the body.
opinions.quote: As bread is the most necessary of all foods, so the thought of death is the most necessary of all works.
original: Ὡς πασῶν τροφῶν ὁ ἄρτος ἀναγκαιότερος, οὕτως πασῶν ἐργασιῶν ἡ τοῦ θανάτου ἔννοια·
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: A lively split: the 'memento mori' revival and Stoic fans agree; many find thinking about death morbid. 'Thinking about my own death every day would make me live better.'

opinions.position: Do not save up money telling yourself it is for the poor. Two small coins bought the kingdom. Whoever has love scatters his money.
opinions.side_note: Against accumulating, even for good causes.
opinions.quote: Do not say that you are gathering money for the sake of the poor; two small coins bought the kingdom.
original: Μὴ λέγε συνάγειν τῶν πτωχῶν ἕνεκα· δύο γὰρ λεπτὰ τὴν βασιλείαν ἠγόρασαν.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Greek in Migne, PG 88
opinions.today: Split: 'give now, do not save up to give later' versus 'build wealth so you can give more'. Fresh and practical.

sparring.over: They accused him of being a chatterbox to stop people coming to him. He answered with silence.
sparring.source: Daniel of Raithu, Life of John Climacus

sparring.with: Monks who slandered others 'out of love'
sparring.over: He rebuked them: 'Stop such love', and told them to pray in secret for the person instead of mocking him.
No real clash with a named early Christian is recorded. He was a peacemaker by reputation, and the record allows only the two episodes above.
