figures.name: Hilary of Poitiers
figures.places: Poitiers in Gaul; exiled to Phrygia in Asia Minor 356-360; the councils of Béziers (356), Seleucia (359) and Constantinople (360); Milan (364)
figures.role: Pagan-born convert and bishop of Poitiers; theologian of the Trinity (On the Trinity), chronicler and fighter in the Arian crisis, one of the first Latin hymn-writers; patron and teacher of Martin of Tours
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches; declared a Doctor of the Church in 1851. His January feast gave its name to the 'Hilary term' at Oxford, at Trinity College Dublin and in the English law courts. Cautions: he writes very dense Latin (Jerome said so); in On the Trinity, Book 10, he argues that Christ's body underwent suffering but did not have 'a nature which could feel pain', a view later theologians did not follow; he called the emperor Constantius Antichrist. Tradition (the Life by Venantius Fortunatus, two centuries later) says he was married with a daughter, Abra; the letter and hymn addressed to Abra are of doubtful authenticity.
figures.hook: Raised a pagan, he found God by reading 'I Am that I Am' in Exodus, became a bishop, was exiled to Asia by the emperor, and was finally sent home by his opponents because they found him too troublesome to keep, 'a sower of discord, and a troubler of the East'.

stories.story: He tells how, as a pagan, he looked for the purpose of life. Wealth and leisure seemed no better than the life of grazing animals, and the philosophers' rules were platitudes. Then he came across the books of Moses and read God's name, 'I Am that I Am', and was amazed. He went on to the Gospel of John and became a Christian.
stories.source: Hilary, On the Trinity, Book 1, sections 1-13 (tr. E.W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899)

stories.story: He admits that although he had been baptized long before and was already a bishop, he had never heard the Nicene Creed until he was on his way into exile. The Gospels and Epistles had taught him what it meant.
stories.source: On the Councils (De Synodis), section 91

stories.story: At the council of Béziers in 356 the party of Bishop Saturninus of Arles had him condemned, and the emperor exiled him to Phrygia. The bishops of Gaul refused communion with Saturninus for the next three years. From exile Hilary wrote that 'the word of God cannot be exiled as our bodies are'.
stories.source: On the Councils, sections 2 and 8; Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, Book 2, chapter 39

stories.story: Still an exile, he was swept along to the council of Seleucia and then to Constantinople, where he publicly asked the emperor for a debate with his opponents. They blocked it, and he was sent back to Gaul 'as being a sower of discord, and a troubler of the East', without his exile being lifted.
stories.source: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, Book 2, chapters 42 and 45 (NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894)

stories.story: Back home, instead of cutting off the many bishops who had signed the compromise creed at Ariminum, he called councils, let them admit the error, and brought them back. Lucifer of Cagliari took the opposite line and broke communion with anyone who readmitted them.
stories.source: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, Book 2, chapter 45

stories.story: A young ex-soldier, Martin (later of Tours), came to live with him. Hilary wanted to make him a deacon, but Martin kept refusing as unworthy, so Hilary, 'a man of deep penetration', gave him the lowly job of exorcist, which Martin could not refuse without seeming proud.
stories.source: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin, chapter 5

stories.story: In Milan in 364 he challenged the Arian bishop Auxentius before the emperor Valentinian's officials. Auxentius declared Christ true God aloud, then handed in a written statement that quietly dodged it. Hilary exposed the trick and was ordered to leave Milan.
stories.source: Hilary, Against Auxentius, sections 7-9 (Latin)

stories.story: Jerome lists among his works 'a book of Hymns', making him one of the first known Latin hymn-writers.
stories.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 100

temperament.evidence: Jerome: 'That reverend man Hilary gains in height from his Gallic buskin; yet, adorned as he is with the flowers of Greek rhetoric, he sometimes entangles himself in long periods and offers by no means easy reading to the less learned brethren.'
Sulpicius says Rhodanius of Toulouse, 'being by nature of a softer disposition, had resisted the Arians, not so much from his own powers as from his fellowship with Hilarius'.
temperament.source: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, Book 2, chapter 39

temperament.evidence: 'Hilarius, as being a man of deep penetration, perceived that he could only be constrained in this way' (on how to get Martin to accept an office).
temperament.source: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin, chapter 5

temperament.evidence: He called the emperor Constantius 'the antichrist' who 'does not flog the back but strokes the belly', and defended himself: it befits ministers of truth to speak the truth.
To the Western bishops about the Easterners: 'I pray you to let there be no conflict of suspicions where there is peace at heart.'

genuine_lines.quote: I know, O Lord God Almighty, that I owe You, as the chief duty of my life, the devotion of all my words and thoughts to Yourself.
genuine_lines.translation: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent (which modernises Thee to You)

genuine_lines.quote: For the word of God cannot be exiled as our bodies are, or so chained and bound that it cannot be imparted to you in any place.
genuine_lines.translation: L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Heresy lies in the sense assigned, not in the word written; the guilt is that of the expositor, not of the text.
genuine_lines.translation: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: It is time to speak, because the time for keeping silent has now passed.
original: Tempus est loquendi: quia jam praeteriit tempus tacendi.
genuine_lines.translation: Own rendering of the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource)

genuine_lines.quote: Though long ago regenerate in baptism, and for some time a bishop, I never heard of the Nicene creed until I was going into exile
genuine_lines.translation: L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: The Letter to his daughter Abra and the morning hymn 'Lucis largitor splendide'
misattributed.truth: Printed among his works, but their authenticity is doubted by most scholars. Do not use them to portray him as a father.

misattributed.line: 'Hammer of the Arians' (malleus Arianorum) as a title from his own day
misattributed.truth: A later honorific; it is not how his contemporaries named him.

opinions.position: Faith should be lived and worshipped in silence. Probing God in words is a trespass that heretics force on us; we speak only because error makes us.
opinions.side_note: Reluctant speculation: the 'mystery, not argument' side.
opinions.quote: The error of others compels us to err in daring to embody in human terms truths which ought to be hidden in the silent veneration of the heart.
opinions.translation: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many think asking hard questions about God is healthy; others feel some things should be left as mystery. Good statement: 'Some questions about God are better left unasked.'

opinions.position: God does not call us to heaven through hard debates or clever rhetoric. The road is plain: believe God raised Jesus and confess He is Lord.
opinions.side_note: Relates to 'questioning' and 'learning'. Striking from a man who wrote twelve dense books on the Trinity.
opinions.quote: For God does not call us to the blessed life through arduous investigations. He does not tempt us with the varied arts of rhetoric. The way to eternity is plain and easy
opinions.translation: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'faith is simple' versus 'faith needs study to be real'. Evangelicals and many others lean simple; academics lean the other way.

opinions.position: A Church that uses exile and prison to make people believe betrays its own past, since it spread through the exiled and imprisoned.
opinions.side_note: Against state force in religion. Aimed at the Arian party backed by the emperor.
opinions.quote: The Church now terrifies with exile and prison, and forces people to believe her, she who was herself believed in amid exiles and prisons.
original: Terret exsiliis et carceribus Ecclesia: credique sibi cogit, quae exsiliis et carceribus est credita.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource)
opinions.today: Almost everyone agrees today that faith must not be forced; strong reveal line, weak statement. A sharper modern statement: 'Laws should not favour one religion.'

opinions.position: God taught people to know Him; He never demanded it by force, and He scorns a confession that is forced.
opinions.side_note: Same side as above. Caution: this passage stands in the work printed as 'Book 1 to Constantius', which modern editors treat as partly a council letter and partly Hilary's own narrative; this sentence is in the narrative part.
opinions.quote: God taught the knowledge of Himself rather than exacting it; winning authority for His commands by the wonder of His heavenly works, He scorned a will forced to confess Him.
original: Deus cognitionem sui docuit potius, quam exegit: et operationum coelestium admiratione praeceptis suis concilians auctoritatem, coactam confitendi se adspernatus est voluntatem.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource)
opinions.today: As above: near-universal agreement today.

opinions.position: There is a time when keeping quiet is cowardice. Staying silent any longer is a sign of lack of faith, not modesty; always keeping silent is as dangerous as never doing so.
opinions.side_note: Against silence when truth is at stake; the opposite pole from Benedict and Climacus.
opinions.quote: For to keep silent any longer is a sign of distrust, not a reasoned modesty; since it is no less dangerous always to have kept silent than never to have done so.
original: Ulterius enim tacere, diffidentiae signum est, non modestiae ratio, quia non minus periculi est semper tacuisse, quam numquam.
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource)
opinions.today: Strong split: 'staying quiet to keep the peace is often cowardice' versus 'wise people hold their tongue'. Excellent statement.

opinions.position: A Christian leader must name a ruler's wrongdoing openly and harshly if needed. A flattering persecutor who buys people with money and honours is worse than one who tortures.
opinions.side_note: Relates to 'state-religion' and 'correction'.
opinions.quote: But now we fight against a persecutor who deceives, an enemy who flatters, against Constantius the antichrist, who does not flog the back but strokes the belly
original: At nunc pugnamus contra persecutorem fallentem, contra hostem blandientem, contra Constantium antichristum: qui non dorsa caedit, sed ventrem palpat
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource)
opinions.today: Very split, and politically charged: some want pastors to speak against rulers, others want them to stay out of politics. Phrase generally: 'Church leaders should publicly condemn powerful leaders who do wrong.'

opinions.position: Do not quarrel over a word when you agree on the thing it means. Look for peace where hearts already agree.
opinions.side_note: The conciliator's side; his rigorist ally Lucifer attacked him for it.
opinions.quote: For it is absurd to fear cavil about a word when the fact expressed by the word presents no difficulty.
opinions.translation: L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'if we mean the same thing, the words do not matter' versus 'words matter; loose words lead to loose beliefs'. Good, everyday statement.

opinions.topic: new: changing beliefs to fit the times
opinions.position: Rewriting the faith every year to suit the moment turns it into 'a faith of the times rather than of the Gospels'. Keep what was received.
opinions.side_note: The 'keep the old faith' side against doctrinal updating.
opinions.quote: And faith has become a thing of the times rather than of the Gospels... We decree yearly and monthly creeds about God; we repent of our decrees; we defend those who repent; we anathematize those we defended.
original: et facta est fides temporum potius quam Evangeliorum
Annuas atque menstruas de Deo fides decernimus, decretis poenitemus, poenitentes defendimus, defensos anathematizamus
opinions.translation: Own rendering of the Latin (Migne text on Latin Wikisource)
opinions.today: A live split: 'churches should update their teaching as society changes' versus 'the faith should never change with the times'. Strong statement.

opinions.position: Wealth with leisure, the life most people want, is not much above the life of grazing animals. Human beings are made for more.
opinions.side_note: Against comfort as the goal of life.
opinions.quote: And yet, though these two embrace the highest and best of the luxuries of life, they seem not far removed from the normal pleasures of the beasts
opinions.translation: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'a comfortable, relaxed life is a good goal' versus 'comfort is not enough to live for'. Good statement.

opinions.position: It is beneath human dignity to think we were born only to feed our greed and laziness; nature itself tells us life aims higher, at immortality.
opinions.quote: nature herself has taught them that it is unworthy of humanity to hold themselves born only to gratify their greed and their sloth
opinions.translation: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree in part; the split is between 'life has a built-in higher purpose' and 'we make our own meaning'.

opinions.position: The philosophers' moral rules were true but shallow, things any animal instinct could grasp. He wanted to know God himself, and found that in Scripture, not in the schools.
opinions.side_note: Values reason but finds philosophy insufficient; Scripture completes the search.
opinions.quote: Their precepts were platitudes, on the mere level of human impulse; animal instinct could not fail to comprehend them
opinions.translation: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'philosophy and self-help are shallow next to Scripture' versus 'wisdom can be found anywhere'.

opinions.position: Scripture is not the problem; bad interpreters are. Heresy is in the meaning people force on the text, not in the text.
opinions.side_note: Defends the plain meaning of the words against arbitrary interpretation.
opinions.quote: Heresy lies in the sense assigned, not in the word written; the guilt is that of the expositor, not of the text.
opinions.translation: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most believers agree; sceptics would say the text itself is the problem. Reveal line.

opinions.position: Those who had signed a heretical creed under pressure should be brought back through repentance, not cut off forever.
opinions.side_note: The generous side; Lucifer of Cagliari took the hard side. Reported by Sulpicius Severus (writing c. 403), not in Hilary's own words.
opinions.quote: he thought the best thing he could do was to bring back all to repentance and reformation.
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'people who caved under pressure deserve a way back' versus 'those who betrayed the cause should not lead again'.

opinions.position: Be humble in your heart, but let your mind and soul aim at the highest things. Humility is not small thinking.
opinions.quote: We must strike a middle course, then, between humility and exaltation, so that we may be humble in heart but lifted up in soul and thought.
opinions.translation: E.W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series, vol. 9 (1899), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'a humble person should not have big ambitions' versus 'humility and big ambitions go together'.

sparring.over: Imperial backing of the Arian party and the exile of bishops. Hilary first petitioned him politely, then wrote Against Constantius calling him Antichrist (c. 360-361; Jerome says it circulated after the emperor's death).
sparring.source: Hilary, To Constantius, Book 2; Against Constantius; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 100

sparring.over: Saturninus's party had Hilary condemned at Béziers and exiled in 356. Hilary says Saturninus acted 'fearing his own conscience' and 'after beguiling the Emperor'.
sparring.source: On the Councils, section 2; To Constantius, Book 2, section 2

sparring.over: A public examination in 364 before imperial officials. Auxentius affirmed orthodoxy aloud and dodged it in writing; Hilary exposed him and was expelled from Milan.

Lucifer objected to Hilary's friendly reading of Eastern creeds in On the Councils, and later refused communion with bishops readmitted after Ariminum, which Hilary had done. Hilary answered his critics in a short apology.
sparring.source: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, Book 2, chapter 45; NPNF introduction to De Synodis

sparring.with: Valens and Ursacius, bishops of the Arian party
sparring.over: He wrote a whole history against them; in On the Councils he doubts they could honestly have misunderstood the word homoousios.
sparring.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 100; On the Councils

sparring.over: Jerome admired him but complained that his style was lofty and hard for ordinary readers.
